questions.q: A lymph node section shows pale-staining channels immediately deep to the capsule. Which structure is being examined?
questions.explain: The subcapsular sinus lies just beneath the lymph-node capsule and receives lymph from afferent lymphatic vessels. It communicates with cortical and medullary sinuses.

questions.q: Which specialised venule allows most circulating lymphocytes to leave the blood and enter a lymph node?
questions.explain: High endothelial venules in the paracortex have specialised endothelial cells that support lymphocyte adhesion and migration from blood into lymph-node tissue.

questions.q: A thymic section contains concentric eosinophilic whorls in its medulla. What are these structures?
questions.explain: Hassall corpuscles are characteristic concentric structures formed by epithelial reticular cells in the thymic medulla.

questions.q: In a lymph node, a secondary follicle with a pale germinal centre is primarily the site of proliferation of which cell population?
questions.explain: Secondary follicles contain germinal centres where activated B cells proliferate and undergo affinity maturation and class switching with support from follicular dendritic cells and helper T cells.

questions.q: Which feature best distinguishes the thymus from a lymph node on routine histology?
options: Lobules with a dark cortex and pale medulla
Numerous lymphoid follicles with germinal centres
A subcapsular sinus receiving afferent lymph
A medulla containing medullary cords and sinuses
questions.explain: The thymus is divided into lobules, each with a densely cellular cortex and a paler medulla. Normal thymic tissue lacks lymphoid follicles and afferent lymphatic vessels.
